\chapter{A Ticket, and a Missed Train}
\label{ch:ru-a-ticket-and-a-missed-train}
\hlchaptermodality{266}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can buy a ticket, \ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}, at the station, follow an announcement, and report a problem: \ru{я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}, \ru{я} \ru{потерял} \ru{билет}.}

Complete RU-C266-review: buy a return ticket at the till, follow an announcement, then report a missed train and a lost ticket.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{билет} \ru{туда} \ru{и} … (bilét tudá i …)}{билет туда и … (bilét tudá i …)}]{\ru{билет} \ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно} (bilét tudá i obrátno) — a return ticket}

\label{lesson:RU-C266-tuda-i-obratno}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}a ticket\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}a train\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}the till\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Bilét. Póyezd. Kássa.}) Then ask the way to the till. (\emph{Kak proytí k kásse?})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}}
\textbf{\ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}} — \emph{tudá i obrátno} — \textquotedblleft{}there and back\textquotedblright{}. At the till it is a return ticket:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{— \ru{Один} \ru{билет} \ru{до} \ru{Москвы}, \ru{пожалуйста}. — \ru{Туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}?} — \emph{odín bilét do Moskvý, pozhálusta. tudá i obrátno?} — One ticket to Moscow, please. Return? \textbf{— \ru{Да}, \ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}.} — \emph{da, tudá i obrátno} — Yes, a return.
\end{quote}

A single is \textbf{\ru{в} \ru{одну} \ru{сторону}} — \emph{v odnú stóronu} — \textquotedblleft{}in one direction\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \ru{до} a place, \ru{на} a train}]
A ticket goes \textbf{\ru{до}} the place, as far as it, and the place changes as it did after \emph{\ru{до}} in the street: \emph{\ru{светофор}}, \emph{\ru{до} \ru{светофора}}; \emph{\ru{Москва}}, \textbf{\ru{до} \ru{Москвы}}.

A ticket is \textbf{\ru{на}} the train or the bus, and \emph{\ru{поезд}} and \emph{\ru{автобус}} keep their plain form: \textbf{\ru{билет} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}}, \textbf{\ru{билет} \ru{на} \ru{автобус}} — \emph{bilét na póyezd, bilét na avtóbus}. After \emph{\ru{два}}, \emph{\ru{билет}} adds \textbf{-\ru{а}}: \textbf{\ru{два} \ru{билета}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{— \ru{Сколько} \ru{стоит} \ru{билет}? — \ru{Тысяча} \ru{рублей}.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Skólko stóit bilét?} — \textquotedblleft{}How much is the ticket?\textquotedblright{} \emph{Týsyacha rubléy} — \textquotedblleft{}A thousand roubles.\textquotedblright{} After \emph{\ru{тысяча}}, \emph{\ru{рубль}} takes the counting form \textbf{\ru{рублей}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{обратно}} is the adverb of \emph{\ru{обратный}}, \textquotedblleft{}reverse, return\textquotedblright{}. EtymDB 2.1 has no entry for \emph{\ru{обратный}}, but takes the verb \emph{\ru{обратить}} back to Proto-Slavic \emph{*ob(v)ortiti}. By the usual account that is \emph{\ru{об}-}, \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{}, with a root of turning, kin to \textbf{\ru{вертеть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn\textquotedblright{}, from Proto-Indo-European \emph{*wert-}: a ticket that turns round. \textbf{\ru{туда}} is \textquotedblleft{}to that place\textquotedblright{}, on the same pointing stem as \emph{\ru{тот}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Odín bilét do Moskvý, pozhálusta.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Tudá i obrátno.} Then a single: \emph{V odnú stóronu.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Dva biléta na póyezd.}
  \item \emph{Answer:} \emph{Skólko stóit bilét?} \emph{Týsyacha rubléy.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}A return ticket\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Билет} \ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}.}}) \textquotedblleft{}A ticket to Moscow\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Билет} \ru{до} \ru{Москвы}.}}) \textquotedblleft{}A ticket for the train\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Билет} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}.}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд} (ya opozdál na …)}{я опоздал на поезд (ya opozdál na …)}]{\ru{я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд} (ya opozdál na póyezd) — I've missed the train}

\label{lesson:RU-C266-opozdal}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}to be late\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}to lose\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Opázdyvat. Teryát.}) Then \textquotedblleft{}a return ticket for the train\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Bilét na póyezd tudá i obrátno.})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{Я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}.} — \emph{ya opozdál na póyezd} — I've missed the train. A woman says \textbf{\ru{Я} \ru{опоздала} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}.}
\end{quote}

Russian says \textquotedblleft{}I was late \textbf{for} the train\textquotedblright{}, with \textbf{\ru{на}}, as on a ticket. \textbf{\ru{Опоздать}} is the perfective partner of \emph{\ru{опаздывать}}: one lateness, and the train is gone.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a problem is a result}]
English often reports a problem with \textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{}: I've lost, it has gone. Russian uses the perfective past, because the result is still true now:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{К} \ru{сожалению}, \ru{я} \ru{потерял} \ru{билет}.} — \emph{k sozhaléniyu, ya poteryál bilét} — Unfortunately I've lost my ticket. \textbf{\ru{Поезд} \ru{уже} \ru{ушёл}.} — \emph{póyezd uzhé ushól} — The train has already left.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ru{Потерял}} is the partner of \emph{\ru{терять}}; \textbf{\ru{ушёл}}, of \emph{\ru{уходить}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{— \ru{Извините}, \ru{у} \ru{меня} \ru{проблема}. \ru{Я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}.} \textbf{— \ru{Ничего}. \ru{Есть} \ru{поезд} \ru{через} \ru{час}.}
\end{quote}

\emph{U menyá probléma} — \textquotedblleft{}I have a problem\textquotedblright{}, literally \textquotedblleft{}at me, a problem\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Nichevó. Yest póyezd chérez chas} — \textquotedblleft{}Never mind. There's a train in an hour.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\ru{Есть}}, \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}, is the present of \emph{\ru{быть}} that Russian does say aloud. When it is serious: \textbf{\ru{Помогите}, \ru{пожалуйста}!}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{опоздать}} is \emph{\ru{о}-} with the root of \textbf{\ru{поздно}}, \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}. EtymDB 2.1 lists \emph{\ru{опоздать}} without a parent, and takes \emph{\ru{поздний}}, \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}, back to Proto-Slavic \emph{*pozdĭnŭ}. The usual account relates that root to Latin \emph{post}, \textquotedblleft{}after\textquotedblright{}; EtymDB itself does not draw the link.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Ya opozdál na póyezd}, then a woman: \emph{Ya opozdála na póyezd.}
  \item \emph{K sozhaléniyu, ya poteryál bilét.}
  \item \emph{Izvinítye, u menyá probléma. Póyezd uzhé ushól.}
  \item a problem of your own at a station, with one perfective verb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I've missed the train\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}.}}) \textquotedblleft{}I've lost my ticket\textquotedblright{}: which aspect? (\textbf{Perfective}, \emph{\textbf{\ru{потерял}}}: it is still lost.) \textquotedblleft{}I have a problem\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{У} \ru{меня} \ru{проблема}.}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{объявление} (obyavléniye)}{объявление (obyavléniye)}]{\ru{объявление} (obyavléniye) — an announcement; a notice}

\label{lesson:RU-C266-obyavleniye}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I've missed the train\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Ya opozdál na póyezd.}) Then ask for a return ticket to Moscow. (\emph{Bilét do Moskvý, tudá i obrátno.}) At a station, a voice from above often tells you first that something has gone wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{объявление}}
\textbf{\ru{объявление}} — \emph{obyavléniye} — \textquotedblleft{}an announcement\textquotedblright{}. At the station it is the voice over the platform:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{На} \ru{вокзале} \ru{объявление}: \ru{поезд} \ru{до} \ru{Москвы} \ru{опаздывает}.} — \emph{na vokzále obyavléniye: póyezd do Moskvý opázdyvayet} — An announcement at the station: the train to Moscow is running late.
\end{quote}

Say it in five beats, \emph{ob-yav-lé-ni-ye}, with the weight on \textbf{-lé-}. The \emph{b} stops before the \emph{y}: \emph{ob-yav}, and not \emph{o-byav}. Russian marks that break with a letter of its own, and the next lesson puts it in your hand.

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{— \ru{Что} \ru{в} \ru{объявлении}? — \ru{Поезд} \ru{до} \ru{Москвы} \ru{опаздывает}.} \textbf{— \ru{Ничего}. \ru{Есть} \ru{поезд} \ru{через} \ru{час}.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Shto v obyavlénii?} — \textquotedblleft{}What's in the announcement?\textquotedblright{} After \textbf{\ru{в}}, the word ends in \textbf{-\ru{нии}}: \emph{v obyavlénii}. The noun is neuter. A notice on a door is an \textbf{\ru{объявление}} too: \emph{na dverí obyavléniye}, \textquotedblleft{}there's a notice on the door\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{объявление}} is the noun of the verb \emph{\ru{объявить}}, \textquotedblleft{}to announce\textquotedblright{}, made with the ending \emph{-\ru{ение}} that turns an action into a thing. \emph{\ru{Объявить}} is \emph{\ru{об}-} with \textbf{\ru{явить}}, \textquotedblleft{}to show, to make appear\textquotedblright{}, the verb behind \emph{\ru{явный}}, \textquotedblleft{}plain, obvious\textquotedblright{}. EtymDB 2.1 does not list \emph{\ru{объявление}} or \emph{\ru{объявить}}, but it takes \emph{\ru{явить}} through Old East Slavic \emph{javiti} back to Proto-Slavic \emph{*aviti}, often written \emph{*javiti}, \textquotedblleft{}to make visible\textquotedblright{}. EtymDB stops there, and gives no older parent. An announcement shows everyone the same thing at once.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Obyavléniye.} Then slowly, in beats: \emph{ob-yav-lé-ni-ye.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Na vokzále obyavléniye: póyezd do Moskvý opázdyvayet.}
  \item \emph{Answer:} \emph{Shto v obyavlénii?} The train is late: \emph{Póyezd opázdyvayet.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the announcement came too late for you: \emph{Ya opozdál na póyezd.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}An announcement\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Объявление}.}}) \textquotedblleft{}In the announcement\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{В} \ru{объявлении}.}}) Where does the weight fall? (On \textbf{-lé-}: \emph{obyavléniye}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{ъ} (tvyórdyy znak)}{ъ (tvyórdyy znak)}]{\ru{ъ} (tvyórdyy znak) — the hard sign inside \ru{объявление}}

\label{lesson:RU-W266-tvyordyy-znak}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ru{щ} and \ru{ь} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ru{объявление}} (\emph{obyavléniye}), \textquotedblleft{}an announcement\textquotedblright{}. You met it a moment ago, at the station. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ru{ъ}}
\textbf{\ru{ъ}} — the \textbf{hard sign}, \emph{tvyórdyy znak}.

It is inside \textbf{\ru{объявление}} (\emph{obyavléniye}), right after \textbf{\ru{об}-}. It looks like \textbf{\ru{ь}} with a short flag at the top left, and like \textbf{\ru{ь}} it has no sound of its own. It keeps the \textbf{\ru{б}} apart from the \emph{y} that \textbf{\ru{я}} carries: \emph{ob-yav-lé-ni-ye}, with a small break after the \emph{b}, and not \emph{o-byav-}.

It turns up mostly where a prefix ending in a consonant meets \textbf{\ru{е}}, \textbf{\ru{ё}}, \textbf{\ru{ю}} or \textbf{\ru{я}}: \textbf{\ru{подъезд}} (\emph{podyézd}), the entrance to a block of flats, is \emph{\ru{под}-} with \emph{-\ru{езд}}; \textbf{\ru{съесть}} (\emph{syest}), \textquotedblleft{}to eat up\textquotedblright{}, is \emph{\ru{с}-} with \emph{\ru{есть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to eat\textquotedblright{}.

Both signs put a \emph{y} before the next vowel. \textbf{\ru{ь}} also softens the consonant, and sits inside a word: \textbf{\ru{семья}} (\emph{semyá}), \textquotedblleft{}a family\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\ru{ъ}} asks for a hard one, and sits after a prefix. Before the spelling reform of 1918 it also closed every word ending in a hard consonant: \textbf{\ru{домъ}} for \textbf{\ru{дом}}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ru{ъ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/RU-W266-tvyordyy-znak-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ru{ъ} is written, stroke by stroke}

Follow the numbered strip: start where movement 1 begins, and let each panel show you the next movement before your pen makes it. Then write \ru{ъ} yourself — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
The strip shows \textbf{where to start this letter and which way to travel}, in one attested order, and names its source beneath it. Teachers vary, so treat it as a sound way in, not the only one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ru{объявление}} and point at \ru{ъ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ru{ъ} three times, saying \emph{tvyórdyy znak} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{ь}, then \ru{ъ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ru{объявление}}, then \textbf{\ru{подъезд}}, aloud, with the small break after the prefix
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ru{ъ}? (The \textbf{hard sign}, \emph{tvyórdyy znak}; it has no sound of its own.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ru{объявление}}, \emph{obyavléniye}, \textquotedblleft{}an announcement\textquotedblright{}.) \textquotedblleft{}A family\textquotedblright{}: \ru{ь} or \ru{ъ}? (\textbf{\ru{ь}}, inside the word: \textbf{\ru{семья}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — a ticket, and a train that left without you}

\label{lesson:RU-C266-review}



\begin{quote}
Ask for one return ticket to Moscow. (\emph{Odín bilét do Moskvý, tudá i obrátno, pozhálusta.})
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three lessons and a letter, and the station can be handled out loud. A ticket goes \textbf{\ru{до}} a place and \textbf{\ru{на}} a train; a return is \textbf{\ru{туда} \ru{и} \ru{обратно}}. An \textbf{\ru{объявление}}, \emph{obyavléniye}, tells the whole station at once, and the hard sign, \emph{tvyórdyy znak}, keeps its \emph{ob-} and \emph{-yav-} apart. And when it goes wrong, the perfective past says what happened and is still true: \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{опоздал} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}}, \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{потерял} \ru{билет}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{— \ru{Извините}, \ru{я} \ru{опоздала} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}. \ru{Как} \ru{пройти} \ru{к} \ru{кассе}?} \textbf{— \ru{Идите} \ru{прямо}, \ru{потом} \ru{налево}.}
\end{quote}

The whole trip so far in two lines: a problem in the perfective, a question about the way, and an answer in two steps.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Izvinítye, ya opozdála na póyezd. Kak proytí k kásse?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Dva biléta na póyezd, tudá i obrátno.}
  \item \emph{Answer:} \emph{Shto v obyavlénii na vokzále?} The train is late: \emph{Póyezd opázdyvayet.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{K sozhaléniyu, ya poteryál bilét.}
  \item \emph{Answer:} \emph{Pochemú ty opozdál?} Explain what happened, then what followed, with \emph{poétomu}
  \item \emph{Answer:} the cashier asks \emph{Tudá i obrátno?} Answer for a single: \emph{Nyet, v odnú stóronu.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}She's missed the train\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Она} \ru{опоздала} \ru{на} \ru{поезд}.}}) \textquotedblleft{}Two tickets for the bus\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Два} \ru{билета} \ru{на} \ru{автобус}.}}) \textquotedblleft{}An announcement\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{\ru{Объявление}.}}) In \emph{obyavléniye}, what keeps \emph{ob-} and \emph{-yav-} apart? (The \textbf{hard sign}, \emph{tvyórdyy znak}, which makes no sound of its own.)
\end{tcolorbox}
